L16016@P394: A.1 NUCLEAR FISSION REACTORS
L16017@P394: Most commercial electric power generation plants produce electricity by converting heat into electricity.
L16018@P394: Typically, these plants heat water to generate steam, and the steam is used to drive a turbine generator. In the
L16019@P394: turbine generator, the energy in the steam is first converted into mechanical energy (spinning a turbine shaft),
L16020@P394: which creates electricity by driving a generator. Fossil plants generate heat through a chemical process; the
L16021@P394: burning of fuels such as natural gas or coal. When fossil fuels are burned, energy is released when the carbon
L16022@P394: in the fossil fuel combines with oxygen and burns. Commercial nuclear power plants generate heat through the
L16023@P394: nuclear fission process. The nuclear fission process occurs at a subatomic level and involves the interaction of
L16024@P394: some component part of the atoms. The following section describes the fission process and its control in a
L16025@P394: nuclear reactor.
L16026@P394: A.1.1 Nuclear Fission
L16027@P394: Nuclear fission is a nuclear reaction caused by the interaction between a free neutron and the nucleus of some
L16028@P394: atoms such as uranium or plutonium. An atom consists of a relatively heavy, positively charged nucleus with a
L16029@P394: number of much lighter, negatively charged particles in various orbits around the nucleus. The nucleus is the
L16030@P394: central part of the atom and consists of subparticles called nucleons. There are principally two types of nucleons:
L16031@P394: neutrons which are electrically neutral and protons which are positively charged. The number of protons in the
L16032@P394: nucleus is called the atomic number of that atom; all atoms of the same element have the same number of protons.
L16033@P394: The total number of nucleons in the nucleus is called the mass number, designated as A. Using X to represent
L16034@P394: the chemical symbol for the element and Z to represent the atomic number, each element is presented as X , X ,
L16035@P394: A A
L16036@P394: Z
L16037@P394: or as “the chemical name” - A. When atoms of an element differ in their number of nucleons, they are called
L16038@P394: isotopes of that element. For example, there are three isotopes of hydrogen: hydrogen with a single proton,
L16039@P394: deuterium with a single proton and a single neutron, and tritium with one proton and two neutrons. Tritium can
L16040@P394: be expressed as H , H , or hydrogen 3. Uranium has an atomic number of 92; that is, each atom has 92 protons. 3 3

L16042@P394: The more common isotopes of uranium have either 143 or 146 neutrons. These two isotopes are designated as
L16043@P394: uranium 238, U , or U (approximately 99 percent of all naturally occurring uranium), and uranium 235, 92
L16044@P394: 238 238
L16045@P394: 92U , or U (approximately 0.7 percent of naturally occurring uranium). These are two of the three naturally 235 235
L16046@P394: occurring isotopes of uranium. In all, there are 18 known isotopes of uranium. Different isotopes of the same
L16047@P394-395: element behave identically chemically, but can have significantly different nuclear characteristics.Draft Environmental Impact Statement for the Production of Tritium in a Commercial Light Water Reactor
L16048@P395: A-2
L16049@P395: Fission, as it occurs in a nuclear power plant, is the process by which the atoms of one element (such as uranium
L16050@P395: or plutonium) are converted into atoms of lighter elements through the capture of a neutron and the subsequent
L16051@P395: “splitting” of the atom’s nucleus (Figure A–1). This results in the release of energy; fission products (atoms of
L16052@P395: the lighter elements), and neutrons. Not all isotopes of an element are capable of fission. For uranium, only 4
L16053@P395: of the 18 known isotopes are capable of fission. Of these four, the two most important isotopes are uranium 235
L16054@P395: and uranium 233.
L16055@P395: Fission produces energy in the form of radiation and the kinetic energy of neutrons and fission products. Most
L16056@P395: of the energy released in the fission process is produced as the kinetic energy of the fission products. Lesser
L16057@P395: amounts are released as the kinetic energy of the neutrons and the energy produced from the radioactive decay
L16058@P395: of the fission products generated in the fission process. It is these forms of energy that are used to heat water in
L16059@P395: the core of a nuclear reactor.
L16060@P395: Fission of an atom is initiated with a single neutron, but can result in the creation of many free neutrons (neutrons
L16061@P395: released from the nucleus). These neutrons can potentially initiate additional fission reactions. When exactly
L16062@P395: one neutron generated in a fission reaction initiates another fission reaction, the process is said to be a critical
L16063@P395: chain reaction. Criticality is an important characteristic of the nuclear power reaction. When a reactor is
L16064@P395: maintained in a critical state, the fission reaction proceeds at a constant rate. Since each fission reaction releases
L16065@P395: approximately the same amount of power, this condition will result in the reactor constantly operating at a steady
L16066@P395: power level. Therefore, it is important to control the number of neutrons available for fission. A critical chain
L16067@P395: reaction is represented in Figure A–2. If a series of fission reactions produce, on average, more than one neutron
L16068@P395: per fission that results in additional fissions, the process is said to be supercritical. In this state, the power level
L16069@P395: of the reactor increases. If, on the other hand, a series of fission reactions produce, on average, less than one
L16070@P395: neutron per fission that results in additional fissions, the process is said to be subcritical. In this condition, the
L16071@P395: power level of the reactor drops until eventually the fission process stops.
L16072@P395: A.1.2 Control of Nuclear Reactions in a Reactor
L16073@P395: Fission is not the only reaction that can take place when a neutron interacts with the nucleus of an atom. One of
L16074@P395: three interactions is possible: (1) the neutron is scattered—i.e., it essentially bounces off the nucleus (an elastic
L16075@P395: collision); (2) the neutron is absorbed—the neutron and atom combine to make the next higher isotope of the
L16076@P395: element; or (3) the neutron is absorbed and initiates a fission reaction. These different reactions are all important
L16077@P395: in the operation of a nuclear reactor. The first reaction, scattering, results in a change in the energy of the free
L16078@P395: neutrons. The second reaction, absorption, results in the loss of neutrons from the reactor. Neutrons that are
L16079@P395: absorbed are not available to initiate fission reactions. As discussed in the preceding paragraphs, the third
L16080@P395: reaction, fission, is the process by which energy is produced in a nuclear reactor and additional neutrons are
L16081@P395: produced to sustain the chain reaction. The likelihood of each of these interactions depends primarily on the
L16082@P395: following two factors: the energy of the free neutrons and the isotope of the atom being struck by the neutron.
L16083@P395: In U.S. commercial nuclear reactors, only uranium 235 is used as the nuclear fuel. Uranium 235 is found
L16084@P395: naturally in uranium ore, although natural uranium consists predominantly of uranium 238. Enriched uranium
L16085@P395: is used in U.S. commercial nuclear power plants. This is uranium in which the percentage of uranium 235 has
L16086@P395: been increased from the less than 1 percent found in natural uranium to 3–5 percent. With approximately
L16087@P395: 100 metric tons of enriched uranium (3–5 metric tons of uranium 235) in the reactor core, a nuclear power plant
L16088@P395: can operate for approximately 18 months without refueling. When the uranium fuel is removed from the reactor,
L16089@P395-396: much of the uranium 235 has been consumed and the spent fuel contains approximately 1 percent uranium 235.Appendix A—Tritium Production Operations–Application to Production of Tritium in Commercial Light Water Reactors

L16094@P397: The fission reaction of a uranium 235 atom produces approximately 2.5 neutrons. Neutrons produced in fission
L16095@P397: are called fast neutrons. This refers to the amount of kinetic energy associated with the neutrons. However, the
L16096@P397: fission process using uranium 235 works better with slower moving neutrons; that is, neutrons with significantly
L16097@P397: less energy than the neutrons produced from the fission process. These neutrons are called thermal neutrons.
L16098@P397: Neutrons are slowed via collisions with nuclei of atoms in the reactor core. In the collisions, energy is transferred
L16099@P397: from the neutron to the atom it collides with. Generally, the closer in weight the neutron and atom are, the more
L16100@P397: energy is transferred to the atom. This transfer of energy from the neutron to other materials results in the
L16101@P397: slowing down of the neutron and is called moderation. The moderator in U.S. commercial nuclear power plants,
L16102@P397: both pressurized and boiling water reactors, is ordinary light water. (Because the moderator used in U.S.
L16103@P397: commercial power reactors is light water and the fission reaction of uranium 235 requires slower moving
L16104@P397: (thermal) neutrons, these types of reactors are referred to as thermal light water reactors.) The hydrogen in light
L16105@P397: water (with a nucleus containing a single proton) is nearly the same mass as the neutron. Collisions between
L16106@P397: neutrons and the hydrogen atoms result in a relatively rapid reduction in the energy of the neutrons. After many
L16107@P397: such collisions, the neutrons are traveling slow enough to be considered thermal neutrons.
L16108@P397: Neutrons that are not lost from the reactor core between the time they are created as fast neutrons and the time
L16109@P397: they are moderated to thermal energy levels are available for fission. Neutrons are lost from the reactor core in
L16110@P397: several ways. Some are lost to leakage; that is, they escape from the reactor core and are captured in the reactor
L16111@P397: vessel or shielding. Some are absorbed by material in the core without producing fission. (Other materials in
L16112@P397: the core, including uranium 238 and core internal structures, contribute to the absorption of neutrons. Some
L16113@P397: neutrons that collide with uranium 235 atoms are absorbed without resulting in fission.) Specific materials,
L16114@P397: referred to as neutron poisons or simply poisons, are inserted in the reactor core to intentionally capture neutrons
L16115@P397: and provide control over the fission rate by controlling the number of neutrons available for fission. Poisons,
L16116@P397: contained in control and shutdown rods, are necessary for several reasons. These devices provide control of the
L16117@P397: rate of fission, thereby controlling the reactor power level. In addition, these devices also allow for the prompt
L16118@P397: termination of fission if the rods are fully inserted into the reactor core, shutting down the reactor. The material
L16119@P397: used in control and shutdown rods is usually boron; a strong neutron absorber. In a collision between boron and
L16120@P397: a neutron, there is a high likelihood that the neutron will be absorbed into the boron, thus generating a different
L16121@P397: boron isotope. Therefore, the position of the control rods determine the power level of the reactor by controlling
L16122@P397: the number of neutrons available for fission.
L16123@P397: Other poisons, called burnable poisons (because during the time the fuel is in the reactor the burnable poisons
L16124@P397: are used up and gradually become less effective as neutron absorbers), are placed in a reactor core in addition to
L16125@P397: the poisons that are contained in the control and shutdown rods. These burnable poisons are necessary for a
L16126@P397: reactor to operate over an extended period without loading fresh fuel into the reactor. Commercial reactors
L16127@P397: typically load fresh fuel once every one to two years. As the power plant operates during this period, uranium
L16128@P397: 235 is burned up (consumed in the fission process or by neutron absorption). Since the source of the neutrons
L16129@P397: is devoured during the generation of power, it is necessary to start the fuel cycle with more uranium 235 than is
L16130@P397: necessary to sustain a critical reaction at the desired power level. Extra uranium 235 is loaded into the reactor
L16131@P397: core, necessitating the use of burnable poisons to keep the power at the appropriate level. The reactor’s power
L16132@P397: levels are controlled by using either fixed burnable poisons (burnable poison rods) in areas that would have higher
L16133@P397: than average free neutron flux or by adding boron (in the form of boric acid) to the coolant in a pressurized water
L16134@P397: reactor. As the fuel burns it becomes less reactive, because less fissionable uranium is available. Since there are
L16135@P397: fewer uranium 235 atoms per unit volume, fewer neutrons are being produced. With fewer neutrons produced,
L16136@P397: the percentage of neutrons lost to leakage and absorption must be reduced to maintain the number of neutrons
L16137@P397: available for fission. Control of neutron loss due to absorption is accomplished by reducing the concentration
L16138@P397-398: of boron in the coolant and the reduction of burnable poison in the burnable absorber rods placed in the core.Appendix A—Tritium Production Operations–Application to Production of Tritium in Commercial Light Water Reactors

L16140@P398: A.2 COMMERCIAL NUCLEAR POWER PLANT DESCRIPTIONS
L16141@P398: A.2.1 Commercial Nuclear Reactors
L16142@P398: In the United States there are two types of commercial nuclear power plants currently in operation; the boiling
L16143@P398: water reactor and the pressurized water reactor.
L16144@P398: The boiling water reactor is a single-loop system. The fission energy in the core causes the water to boil in the
L16145@P398: reactor vessel. In the reactor vessel, above the fuel, the steam passes through steam separators and steam dryers,
L16146@P398: which are used to ensure dry steam exits the reactor vessel, and travels through steam pipes to the turbine
L16147@P398: generator. The steam drives the turbine, which in turn powers the generator to create electricity. As steam passes
L16148@P398: through the turbine, it loses most of its energy but remains as steam as it passes to the main condenser. In the
L16149@P398: main condenser, where additional heat is removed by a cooling water system, the steam condenses into water.
L16150@P398: This water is pumped back to the reactor vessel where it is forced through the reactor core and is again converted
L16151@P398: to steam. Figure A–3 provides a simplified representation of a boiling water reactor. Boiling water reactors
L16152@P398: typically operate at pressures of approximately 70 kilograms/meter (1,000 pounds/inch ), and the temperature 2 2
L16153@P398: of the water and steam in the reactor vessel approaches 288
L16154@P398: A pressurized water reactor uses a primary and secondary system to transfer heat from the reactor core to the
L16155@P398: turbine generator (see Figure A–4 for a simplified representation of a pressurized water reactor). In the primary
L16156@P398: loop (the reactor coolant system) water is forced up through the core, where it is heated but does not boil. After
L16157@P398: the water exits the reactor vessel it passes through steam generators. The number of steam generators used in
L16158@P398: the power plant depends on the design and power level. Combustion Engineering and Babcock & Wilcox designs
L16159@P398: have two steam generators. Westinghouse designs can have from two to four steam generators. The more recent
L16160@P398: (larger power plants) have four steam generators (Figure A–5 is an isometric of a Representative Reactor FourLoop Primary System). Each steam generator is connected to the reactor vessel in a separate, independent coolant
L16161@P398: loop. In the steam generators, the primary coolant heats water in the secondary loop and converts the water to
L16162@P398: steam. After the primary coolant leaves the steam generator, it is pumped back to the reactor vessel where it is
L16163@P398: again heated in the reactor core. The primary system has a pressurizer, which is used to control the pressure of
L16164@P398: the primary system. The pressurizer is connected to one of the primary loops and is located above the reactor
L16165@P398: core. It contains heaters and sprays that are used to control the water level in the pressurizer which, in turn,
L16166@P398: controls the pressure of the primary coolant system. The steam in the secondary loop (referred to as the steam
L16167@P398: and power conversion system) is used to drive the turbine generator and produce electricity. As in the boiling
L16168@P398: water reactor, after the steam passes through the turbine it is condensed by cooling water in the main condenser.
L16169@P398: This cooled water is then pumped back to the secondary side of the steam generator. A pressurized water reactor
L16170@P398: primary system operates at pressures of about 158 kilograms/meter (2,250 pounds/inch ) and temperatures of 2 2
L16171@P398: up to approximately 315 F), with the secondary loop operating at approximately 70 kilograms/meter2
L16172@P398: (1,000 pounds/inch ) and 288 2
L16173@P398: In addition to the difference in the number of cooling loops associated with a boiling water reactor and a
L16174@P398: pressurized water reactor, there are some differences in the design of the reactor cores. In a pressurized water
L16175@P398: reactor, the control and shutdown rods enter the reactor core from above. In a boiling water reactor these rods
L16176@P398: are driven into the core (via a control rod driven system) from the bottom of the core. Also, pressurized water
L16177@P398: reactors use soluble neutron poison (a boric acid solution) in the primary coolant to help control reactivity. The
L16178@P398: concentration of the soluble neutron poison is controlled by the chemical and volume control system. Typically,
L16179@P398: the concentration of boric acid is highest at the beginning of a fuel cycle when there is fresh fuel in the core. A
L16180@P398-399: boiling water reactor does not use this means of reactivity control.Draft Environmental Impact Statement for the Production of Tritium in a Commercial Light Water Reactor

L16186@P400: A.2.2 Reactor Core Description
L16187@P400: Fuel in a nuclear reactor is slightly enriched (up to 5 percent) uranium dioxide and is sealed in fuel rods. These
L16188@P400: rods are approximately 3.6 to 3.9 meters (12 to 13 feet) long and slightly less than a half inch in diameter.
L16189@P400: Uranium, in the form of approximately half-inch long cylindrical uranium dioxide pellets, is placed in a fuel rod
L16190@P400: and enclosed in a zircaloy cladding. This cladding holds the pellets in position and provides a barrier against the
L16191@P400-401: release of fission products into the reactor coolant system.Draft Environmental Impact Statement for the Production of Tritium in a Commercial Light Water Reactor
L16192@P401: A-8
L16193@P401: In a pressurized water reactor, the fuel rods are collected in a fuel assembly that also contains several guide tubes
L16194@P401: and an instrumentation channel (illustrated in Figure A–6). The number of fuel rods in an assembly varies
L16195@P401: depending on the design of the reactor. Assemblies contain fuel rods arranged in 14 × 14, 15 × 15, or 17 × 17
L16196@P401: arrays. The more recent reactors tend to use the 17 × 17 array. The guide tubes denote the location where the
L16197@P401: control rods of the control element assemblies are inserted into the reactor core. The fuel rods, guide tubes, and
L16198@P401: the instrumentation channel are held in place by a series of grids at several locations along the full length of the
L16199@P401: fuel assembly. In a reactor core, fuel assemblies are all structurally identical and have space reserved for control
L16200@P401: element assemblies. In the Westinghouse designs, between a third and a fourth of the fuel assemblies have an
L16201@P401: associated control element assembly. In a large pressurized water reactor, one with an electrical power rating of
L16202@P401: over 1,000 megawatts, the core will consist of approximately 200 fuel assemblies. Of these, 50 to 60 fuel
L16203@P401: assemblies (depending on the reactor design) have associated control element assemblies. The remaining fuel
L16204@P401: assemblies may have burnable poison rods in the locations used by control element assemblies, or these locations
L16205@P401: may be empty. The burnable poison rods are rods with the same shape as the control and shutdown rods.
L16206@P401: However, they are not connected to the control rod-driven mechanism and cannot be removed from the reactor
L16207@P401: without shutting it down and performing refueling activities that involve removing the fuel assembly containing
L16208@P401: the burnable poison rods from the reactor core. Loading of the burnable poison rods in these locations for the
L16209@P401: assemblies without control element assemblies is dictated by the need to balance the power distribution in the
L16210@P401: core.
L16211@P401: The control element assembly consists of a collection of control rods and a spider assembly at the top of the rods.
L16212@P401: Figure A–7 shows a control element assembly for a Representative Reactor 17 × 17 fuel assembly design. The
L16213@P401: spider assembly is connected to a control rod drive mechanism that can be used to move the control element
L16214@P401: assemblies. These assemblies serve two purposes—to limit the effects of reactivity changes during power
L16215@P401: operation and to shutdown the reactor. The rods are made of a strong neutron absorber (typically a boron or
L16216@P401: cadmium compound). When not needed, the control element assemblies are pulled out of the core by their control
L16217@P401: rod drives. For reactivity control during operation, the control rod drive can be used to insert the rods into the
L16218@P401: core at a controlled pace. If needed, the rods can be rapidly inserted to shut down the reactor. It is possible for
L16219@P401: the control element assemblies to be inserted into the core using only the force of gravity as the driving force.
L16220@P401: When fully inserted, the poison in the control rods absorbs enough neutrons to make the nuclear reaction become
L16221@P401: subcritical, shutting down the reactor.
L16222@P401: As mentioned earlier, one of the ways in which neutrons are lost from the core and become unavailable for fission
L16223@P401: is through leakage. The neutrons leak from the edges of the core, and those that do not hit an atom and reflect
L16224@P401: back into the core are lost. (Reactor core designs address this problem of neutron loss by incorporating a neutron
L16225@P401: reflector, a layer of water around the core.) Neutrons generated at the center of the core are less likely to be lost
L16226@P401: through leakage than those generated at the edge of the core. Therefore, in a reactor with no burnable poisons
L16227@P401: and a uniform fuel enrichment, the number of neutrons available for fission is greater at the center of the core.
L16228@P401: The center of the core, which is about 3 meters (10 feet) in diameter and 3.6 to 3.9 meters (12 to 13 feet) tall, has
L16229@P401: a higher power density than the areas at the top, bottom, and edge of the core.
L16230@P401: Designers of the reactor core control the distribution of power within the reactor core by using burnable poisons
L16231@P401: and varied fuel rod enrichments. Figure A–8 displays a possible arrangement of fuel assemblies within a reactor
L16232@P401: core. Other fuel loading patterns also exist, but the concept is fully expressed by a simple loading pattern
L16233@P401: described here. This figure shows fresh fuel (typically with the highest enrichment of uranium 235) loaded
L16234@P401: around the core periphery. Fuel in the center of the core is referred to as once or twice burned fuel and has been
L16235@P401: in the core for one or two fuel cycles. A fuel cycle is the period from one refueling outage to another. The older
L16236@P401: fuel in the reactor core has been producing power for one to two years and has burned up some of its uranium
L16237@P401: 235. This fuel is no longer as enriched as the fresh fuel. With less material available for fission in this fuel, the

L16247@P405: The burnable poison rods will be replaced with TPBARs in a tritium production facility (see Section A.3). The

L16252@P405: A.2.3 Reactor Refueling
L16253@P405: Unlike fossil-fueled electricity-generating plants that are continually fuel fed, nuclear power plants operate over
L16254@P405: extended periods without the need for fresh fuel. Typically, reactors will operate for 12 to 18 months between
L16255@P405: refueling outages. As stated earlier, as the uranium 235 is burned up, the reactor becomes increasingly less able
L16256@P405: to maintain a critical condition. Eventually, when enough fuel is burned up, the reactor will not be able to remain
L16257@P405: critical even if all of the neutron poisons are removed from the core. Before this point is reached, the reactor is
L16258@P405: shut down and refueled. When the power plant is shut down during the refueling outage, some (between one-third
L16259@P405: and two-fifths) of the fuel assemblies are removed and replaced with fresh fuel, and some of the assemblies are
L16260@P405: shuffled to different locations within the reactor core. The removed fuel is called spent fuel. The refueling outage
L16261@P405: usually lasts less than two months, during which various maintenance activities are performed. The reactor
L16262@P405: refueling is a small fraction of the overall outage.
L16263@P405: Spent fuel is stored onsite in a spent fuel pool, located in a separate building attached to the containment
L16264@P405: structure. The spent fuel is stored onsite for several years, allowing the assemblies to cool and the radioactivity
L16265@P405: levels to drop sufficiently so that the spent fuel can be safely transported to a temporary or permanent waste
L16266@P405: disposal site.
L16267@P405: The refueling operation of a nuclear power plant can be divided into four separate phases: preparation, reactor
L16268@P405: disassembly, fuel handling, and reactor assembly.
L16269@P405: Preparation
L16270@P405: During preparation, the reactor is shut down, all control and shutdown rods are inserted into the reactor core, and
L16271@P405: the nuclear chain reaction is stopped. Heat is still generated in the reactor core, principally by the radioactive
L16272@P405: decay of the fission products. The amount of heat produced during decay gradually decreases, and the reactor
L16273@P405: is brought to a condition called cold shutdown where the average reactor coolant temperature is below the boiling
L16274@P405: point of water at atmospheric pressure.
L16275@P405: Reactor Disassembly
L16276@P405: The area above the reactor vessel is referred to as the reactor cavity, illustrated in Figure A–9. Adjacent to this
L16277@P405: cavity is the refueling cavity. During reactor disassembly, these two cavities are flooded with borated water to
L16278@P405: provide a medium for the transfer of spent and new fuel. The water provides a means to remove heat from the
